mainKeyword: best low wattage space heater for rv
guideTitle: Best Low Wattage Space Heaters for RVs (2026)
metaTitle: Best Low Wattage RV Space Heaters for 2026
metaDescription: Six low wattage space heaters for RVs, from 250 to 800 watts, compared by amp draw, thermostat control and safety so they fit a crowded 30 amp circuit.
expertTake: The Brightown 800W plug-in is the best low wattage pick because its 300 watt first step and ECO routine let you tune the load, and the Amazon Basics 500W is the value pick. Anyone heating a full-length trailer from one unit needs more than 800 watts and should skip this category.
introParagraphs: A low wattage heater trades peak output for breathing room on the breaker. In an RV the pedestal might supply 30 amps in total, and the air conditioner, microwave and water heater element all want a share of it.

The aim here is a heater that fits beside those loads without tripping anything. That means accepting limited reach: these units warm a bunk, a bath or a corner, and they do it for a few amps instead of a dozen.

products.name: Brightown 800W Plug-In Heater with Remote and ECO Mode
products.description:
Brightown builds an 800 watt plug-in heater with a 300 watt first step, a second 800 watt step and an ECO mode. That 300 watt setting is the useful one for a crowded RV circuit, since it draws only about 2.5 amps and still takes the edge off a cool night. The unit plugs into a wall outlet and comes with a remote and an LED display.

The listing claims it warms spaces up to 100 square feet, which is a realistic figure for 800 watts at roughly 8 watts per square foot. ETL certification gives some assurance on the safety side, covering overheat and tip-over protection. Next to the 500 watt Gaiatop, it offers more headroom for cold nights and finer control.

Because it sits on the outlet, make sure the receptacle holds it firmly. Wipe the vents with a dry cloth once a month. A warm plug is the signal to stop using it and replace the unit. Run the ECO mode first in a new rig for a night or two, watch how often it cycles, and adjust the placement until it holds the bunk comfortable on the 300 watt step alone.
products.bestFor: RV owners who want fine control over a small load.
pros: 300W first step draws only about 2.5 amps
Remote and LED display for bedtime control

products.name: Teioe 800W/400W Mini PTC Ceramic Heater
products.description:
Teioe's mini heater has two power steps, 800 and 400 watts, in a body that weighs 1.6 pounds and measures 8.3 by 5.5 by 3.1 inches. The PTC ceramic element limits its own temperature, and the casing is flame-retardant. It is built to sit on a desk, a counter or a bedside table.

The 400 watt step draws about 3.3 amps, which is easy on a shared circuit, and the 800 watt step doubles it for colder mornings. Compared with Brightown it lacks a remote and a thermostat, so control is manual. It is simpler and more portable.

Its light weight makes it travel friendly, but light also means it can slide on a slick surface. Set it on a non-slip mat while driving only if you stow it. Keep it away from bedding and clean the grille regularly. Owners who like this style often buy a second unit for the other end of the rig instead of one big heater, which spreads the load across two outlets and two circuits.
products.bestFor: Simple two-step warmth on a desk or bedside.
cons: Limited reach in a large cabin

products.name: DR.PREPARE 600W PTC Ceramic Heater with Adjustable Tilt
products.description:
This 600 watt heater adds a manual tilt, from 10 degrees down to 40 degrees up, so you can aim warmth at your feet, a bed or a seat. That is a practical feature in a cramped RV where the heater sits on a low shelf or a stool. The housing uses V-0 flame retardant material.

At about 5 amps it sits between the 400 watt and 800 watt options for amp draw. Aiming the output means you can feel the warmth with a lower setting, which makes the 600 watt rating go further than it sounds. Against the Gaiatop at 500 watts, it adds tilt and a slightly higher ceiling.

Measuring 5.4 by 5.3 by 7.8 inches, it fits a cupboard shelf. Check that the tilt hinge holds its angle during use, because a hinge that creeps downward ends up blowing warm air at the floor. Hinge friction is the part that wears first on any tilting small heater. Vacuum the intake each season.
products.bestFor: Aiming warmth at a bed or seat from a low spot.
pros: Tilt adjusts from 10 degrees down to 40 up
cons: Tilt hinge is a mechanical wear point

products.name: Gaiatop 500W Mini PTC Desk Heater
products.description:
Gaiatop's 500 watt desk heater uses a PTC ceramic element and claims warmth in two seconds, which is typical for a small PTC unit. A 45 degree tip-over switch cuts power if it falls. Its sleek, compact shape suits a desk or a nightstand.

At about 4.2 amps it leaves most of a 30 amp circuit free. The trade is that 500 watts is a personal heater, not a room heater, so think in terms of a bunk or a dinette seat. Beside the Performance Tool, it doubles the output for the same kind of use.

Because it is light, keep it on a stable surface and away from the edge. Dust the intake monthly. Replace it if the cord jacket cracks. In a rig that bounces over washboard roads, stowing it in a padded drawer matters more than the brand name on the box.
products.bestFor: Warming one seat or bunk on a tight circuit.
pros: Warms quickly as a small PTC unit
cons: Fan is audible in a silent cabin

products.name: Amazon Basics 500W Ceramic Mini Space Heater
products.description:
Amazon Basics sells a plain 500 watt ceramic mini heater that measures 5.87 by 3.15 by 5.95 inches. It heats in seconds and has built-in tip-over protection that shuts it off if knocked over. The listing calls the operation quiet.

It is the least costly way into low wattage heating in this roundup, and it behaves the way the 500 watt Gaiatop does. The difference is the brand's wide service network. Neither has a thermostat, so you switch it on and off yourself.

Its tiny body goes in a drawer at season's end. Keep the cord uncoiled while it runs and inspect the plug each season. Use it as a boost, not a main heater, and it will serve for years. It pairs well with a bedside timer plug, so a forgotten switch does not leave a heater running while you are out hiking.
products.bestFor: Budget shoppers who need a basic personal heater.
pros: 500W stays easy on a 30 amp circuit
Small body stows in a drawer

products.name: Performance Tool W5011 250W Personal Space Heater
products.description:
Performance Tool's W5011 is a 250 watt personal heater, the lowest output in this roundup and a true foot warmer. At about 2.1 amps it can run alongside almost anything else in an RV without a thought. The listing gives few details beyond its size class, so judge it as a basic, no-frills unit.

That low output defines what it can do: warm your feet under a table, take the chill off a closet or keep a tiny bathroom from feeling icy. It will not change the temperature of a cabin. Set against the 500 watt Gaiatop, it has half the heat and half the draw.

Since the spec sheet is thin, inspect the plug and cord when it arrives and run it where you can watch it for the first hour. Keep it off carpet and away from fabric. Think of it as an accessory to a real heater. It also makes a sensible pet-corner or wet-bay warmer, where all you want is a few degrees above freezing without any real load on the pedestal.
products.bestFor: Foot warming where almost no spare amps exist.
pros: Easy to run with other loads
cons: Too little output for a room

buyingCriteria.criterion: Count the amps, not just watts
buyingCriteria.explanation: Amps equal watts divided by 120 volts. A 250 watt unit draws about 2.1 amps, a 500 watt about 4.2, a 600 watt about 5 and an 800 watt about 6.7. On a 30 amp service shared with an air conditioner, those differences decide whether the breaker holds.

At about 10 watts per square foot, 500 watts covers roughly 50 square feet and 800 watts about 80. Brightown's listing claims 100 square feet for 800 watts. Treat these units as zone heaters for a bunk, a bath or a desk, and think of the main furnace or a larger heater as the base layer. A common error is buying three small units and still being cold, when one properly sized heater would have done the job.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Look for stepped or ECO output
buyingCriteria.explanation: Brightown has a 300 watt first step and an ECO mode, and Teioe offers 400 and 800 watt steps. Steps let you match output to the night, running low in shoulder season and high only when it dips. A single-power heater is all or nothing, so it cycles harder and gives you less say over how the cabin feels. A single-power heater is all or nothing.

All six list tip-over protection, and Gaiatop specifies a 45 degree switch. A light heater slides and tips easily, so this protection is the key safety feature. ETL on the Brightown adds certification assurance.

Plug-in wall heaters hang from the receptacle. A loose or worn outlet can overheat under that weight. Check the socket grips firmly and feels cool after an hour. Never use a power strip or a thin extension cord to get around a poorly placed outlet, since the plug end is where heat builds up.

A small heater works best close to you. The DR.PREPARE tilts from 10 degrees down to 40 up to aim warmth. Keep three feet from bedding and curtains, and avoid putting any of these units on a soft cushion where the vents can be blocked.

howWeEvaluated.title: Amp draw
howWeEvaluated.description: We converted each wattage to amps at 120 volts and compared it with a shared 30 amp circuit. The 250 watt Performance Tool draws about 2.1 amps and the 800 watt units about 6.7. Lower draw scored higher for sharing, but only when the heater could still make a noticeable difference in the space it was meant for.

howWeEvaluated.title: Control options
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for steps, ECO modes, remotes and thermostats. Brightown leads with a remote and ECO. Simple switches scored lower but are fine for short use. We also noted that a remote is only useful if you keep the batteries fresh and the unit within clear reach of the sensor.

howWeEvaluated.title: Reach and aim
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered how well each unit warms a person rather than a room. Tilting heads and a 800 watt ceiling scored higher. Pure personal heaters were scored for their limited zone.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety
howWeEvaluated.description: We confirmed tip-over and overheat protection in each listing. Where certification was named, we credited it. Where the listing said little, as with the 250 watt unit, we advised a cautious first run. Based on owner feedback patterns, warm plugs are the main caution.

howWeEvaluated.title: Portability
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared weight and footprint. Teioe weighs 1.6 pounds and DR.PREPARE fits a small shelf. Lighter units are easier to stow but slide more easily. A thin rubber shelf liner under any of them is a cheap fix.

faq.q: Can a low wattage heater warm a whole RV?
faq.a: Not a full-length trailer. At roughly 10 watts per square foot, 800 watts covers about 80 square feet. Use it for a bunk, bath or small zone, and let the furnace or a larger unit carry the rest of the rig.

faq.q: How many amps does a small heater draw?
faq.a: Divide watts by 120. A 500 watt heater draws about 4.2 amps and an 800 watt heater about 6.7.

faq.q: Is it safe to run one overnight?
faq.a: Use a unit with tip-over and overheat protection and keep it three feet from bedding. A timer or thermostat adds safety.

faq.q: Do low wattage heaters save money?
faq.a: They use less power per hour but may run longer to reach the same warmth. They save most when used as zone heaters.

faq.q: Will a plug-in heater damage the outlet?
faq.a: A firm receptacle handles it well. A loose or worn socket can overheat, so check it feels cool after an hour.

faq.q: Can I run one from an inverter?
faq.a: Short periods are possible with a large battery bank and a sufficient inverter. An hour at 500 watts uses about 40 amp-hours at 12 volts.
